title: A* pathfinding for game NPCs
learner_summary: A computer science undergraduate who writes Python and has built a small 2D grid game in Pygame. They know breadth-first search from a data structures course: a grid as a graph, a tile's neighbors, and a queue of tiles to visit. They have had one short session on A*'s g, h and f values, and they want the guard NPCs in their game to chase the player around walls.

objectives.text: Calculate g(n), h(n), and f(n) in a simple A* example.
Explain the open set, closed set, and node expansion.
Explain how heuristic choice affects efficiency and optimality.

facts.text: g(n) is the cost of the cheapest path found so far from the start to node n.
h(n) is a heuristic estimate of the cost of getting from node n to the goal.
f(n) = g(n) + h(n) is the estimated cost of the cheapest path from the start to the goal that passes through n.
On a grid where an NPC moves only up, down, left or right and every step costs 1, the standard heuristic is Manhattan distance, |dx| + |dy|.
A neighbor's g value along a path is the current node's g value plus the cost of the step from the current node to that neighbor.
The open set holds the nodes that have been discovered but not yet expanded, and A* always expands the open node with the lowest f value next.

To expand a node, A* removes it from the open set and, for each neighbor, computes a tentative g value; when that value is lower than any g value already known for the neighbor, A* records the new g, f and parent and puts the neighbor in the open set.

The closed set holds the nodes that have already been expanded; with a consistent heuristic, such as Manhattan distance on a 4-connected grid with step cost 1, a closed node's g value is final and the node is never expanded again.
A* stops when it selects the goal from the open set for expansion, not when it first adds the goal to the open set; stopping at first discovery can return a path that is not the cheapest.
The path is rebuilt by following parent pointers from the goal back to the start.
If the open set becomes empty before the goal is selected for expansion, no path to the goal exists.

A heuristic is admissible when it never overestimates the true remaining cost to the goal; with an admissible heuristic A* returns a cheapest path, and in the version with a closed set the heuristic must also be consistent, or closed nodes must be reopened when a cheaper path to them is found.
With h(n) = 0 for every node, A* behaves like Dijkstra's algorithm: it still finds a cheapest path, but it usually expands more nodes.
A more informative consistent heuristic, one that is never smaller than another and so closer to the true remaining cost, generally leads A* to expand fewer nodes.

Weighted A* ranks nodes by f = g + w*h with w > 1; it usually expands fewer nodes but may return a path that is not the cheapest, and its path is guaranteed to cost at most w times the cheapest only when step costs are non-negative and h is admissible, with closed nodes reopened when a cheaper path to them is found, or h is consistent.

On a grid where a straight step costs 1 and a diagonal step costs the square root of 2 (about 1.41), Manhattan distance overestimates (one diagonal step to (1,1) costs about 1.41, but Manhattan gives 2), so it is not admissible; octile distance, max(dx, dy) + (sqrt(2) - 1) * min(dx, dy), equals the exact cost on an open grid and is admissible.

On a 4-connected grid with step cost 1, Euclidean and Manhattan distance are both admissible and consistent and Euclidean is never larger, so as a general tendency A* with Euclidean expands at least as many nodes as with Manhattan, though the exact counts in one search can differ among tied nodes depending on how ties in f are broken.

misconceptions.text: A* picks the node that looks closest to the goal, by h alone.
misconceptions.correction: A* ranks open nodes by f = g + h, so the cost already spent to reach a node counts as much as the estimate of what is left.

misconceptions.text: g(n) is the straight-line or grid distance from the start to n.
misconceptions.correction: g(n) is the cost of the path the search actually found from the start to n, including every detour around walls.

misconceptions.text: h(n) is the exact remaining cost, so f(n) is the exact length of the final path.
misconceptions.correction: h(n) is only an estimate; an admissible heuristic is a lower bound, so the real path through n can cost more than f(n).

misconceptions.text: A* can stop as soon as the goal is added to the open set.
misconceptions.correction: A* stops when the goal is selected from the open set for expansion; a cheaper path to the goal may still be found before then.

misconceptions.text: Once a node is in the open set, its g value never changes.
misconceptions.correction: If a cheaper path to an open node is found, A* updates its g, its f and its parent.

misconceptions.text: A larger heuristic is always better, and overestimating only makes A* faster with no downside.
misconceptions.correction: An overestimating heuristic can make A* return a path that is not the cheapest; it trades path quality for speed.

misconceptions.text: Manhattan distance is admissible on any grid.
misconceptions.correction: When diagonal moves are allowed, Manhattan distance can overestimate the remaining cost; octile distance is the admissible choice there.
